why: An unsolicited vendor on a domain registered 13 days ago asks for the current PO number and the name of the invoice approver, which is reconnaissance for invoice fraud.
A prospective client on a long-established mail provider explains a slot he booked through her public intro page, with no link, attachment or request beyond saying whether he fits.
A password-change notice from an established domain with no link or ask, which points her to her normal sign-in screen or administrator if the change was not hers.
A supplier invoice sent to her personal address with new bank details and a payment deadline, justified by a bouncing firm mailbox, is classic payment-diversion fraud built from her team page.
An unsolicited appearance fee for her podcast episode from a sponsor whose domain is three weeks old is a pretext to harvest payee and bank details.
The sender is the association's established address, but it attaches draft minutes of a 6 November meeting that has not yet happened, so she should confirm with Beatrix before opening the attachment.
The forum's established production address announces the recording and a public clip hosted on its own domain, asks for nothing, and needs no reply.
The association secretary, writing from its 2010 domain, asks her by reply to confirm a register entry that holds only public details, with no link, payment or credential involved.
A booking-page prospect on a four-week-old domain sends a password-protected archive, with the password taken from her talk title and a fallback download link, which is a malware-delivery pattern.
A flattering board-seat approach tailored to her role, tenure, CFA and talk comes from a search firm whose domain is one month old and pushes her off email to an unverified phone number.
A colleague on the firm's own domain explains the agency-built microsite domain and asks only for comments on her bio, with no credential or payment request.
A filing notice from a long-established registry domain contains no link or contact to call, and tells her to reply only through the address on her last registry letter, a channel she already knows.
A recruiter on a domain registered in 2009 asks if she will act as referee for a former colleague and wants only a call time, with no link, attachment or money involved.
An alumni-magazine pretext stitched together from her school, talk, podcast and team photo comes from a domain under a month old and urges her to open an attached document by Wednesday.
A class-network mention notification from a domain registered in 2022 links only to its own site and asks for no credentials, money or files.
A flattering nomination on a three-week-old domain asks her to register with her work email and a password and to import her network profile before a 10-day lapse, which is credential harvesting.
An internal colleague on the firm's domain sends the board pack for mark-up, with no external link, payment or credential request.
A text from someone who knows the association's people asks if she could present a report at the AGM and to call when convenient, with no link, money or urgency.
A domain-renewal final notice from an unaffiliated six-week-old domain, with a 3-day deadline and payment link, is a domain-slamming solicitation and not her registrar.
A regatta entry confirmation from an event domain registered two months ago states the fee is already paid and asks for nothing, linking only to its own sailing instructions.

A hosting platform asks a guest to sign in and answer a rights claim under a 5-day deadline that makes the restriction permanent, which is a credential-phish shape, so she should check with the show directly first.
The show's producer, writing from the podcast's established domain, asks only for a yes or no on reusing a clip, with no link or attachment.
A CPD notice from a four-week-old domain that is not her institute threatens an audit and attaches a macro document she is told to enable, which is malware delivery.
A lookalike IT domain registered five days ago demands same-day re-authentication with her work password and MFA through its own sign-in link, which is credential and MFA phishing.
A colleague impersonation on a lookalike domain registered six days ago asks for an urgent GBP 18,750 transfer from the office account with retrospective approval, which is classic CEO fraud.
Her association is impersonated from a two-week-old domain, not its real one, with a survey link that closes today, which is a phishing lure built from her affiliation and location.
A member newsletter from an institute domain dating from 2008 repeats public facts about her talk and podcast, and links only to its own site with no ask.
The association secretary, writing from its long-standing domain, invites views on the consultation with a reasonable deadline and an explained collection page, and asks for no credentials or money.
